title: Chapter IX

teacherSummary.text: Tormented by guilt, Victor considers suicide. His family withdraws to Belrive. Victor journeys into the Alps toward Chamounix, where the majesty of mountains, glaciers and Mont Blanc offers temporary relief.

vocabulary.context: I passed the bridge of Pélissier, where the ravine, which the river forms, opened before me, and I began to ascend the mountain that overhangs it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overhang”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To cause to rest by soothing influences
vocabulary.context: The same lulling sounds acted as a lullaby to my too keen sensations: when I placed my head upon my pillow, sleep crept over me; I felt it as it came, and blessed the giver of oblivion.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “lull”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: An immense field or stream of ice, formed in the region of perpetual snow, and moving slowly down a mountain slope…
vocabulary.context: Immense glaciers approached the road; I heard the rumbling thunder of the falling avalanche, and marked the smoke of its passage.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “glacier”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I had been the author of unalterable evils; and I lived in daily fear, lest the monster whom I had created should perpetrate some new wickedness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “perpetrate”: per- (Latin per, "through, thoroughly") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A large mass or body of snow and ice sliding swiftly down a mountain side, or falling down a precipice
vocabulary.context: Immense glaciers approached the road; I heard the rumbling thunder of the falling avalanche, and marked the smoke of its passage.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “avalanche”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Beginning and ending in a day
vocabulary.context: It was during an access of this kind that I suddenly left my home, and bending my steps towards the near Alpine valleys, sought in the magnificence, the eternity of such scenes, to forget myself and my ephemeral, because human, sorrows.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ephemeral”: -al (Latin -alis, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: At these moments I wept bitterly, and wished that peace would revisit my mind only that I might afford them consolation and happiness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “revisit”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + vis (Latin videre, "to see"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A sensation of dryness in the throat associated with a craving for liquids, produced by deprivation of drink, or by…
vocabulary.context: I had begun life with benevolent intentions, and thirsted for the moment when I should put them in practice, and make myself useful to my fellow-beings.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “thirst”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To kill by surprise or secret assault
vocabulary.context: William and Justine were assassinated, and the murderer escapes; he walks about the world free, and perhaps respected.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “assassinate”: as- (Latin ad, "to") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To give up, the will, courage, or spirit
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth was sad and desponding; she no longer took delight in her ordinary occupations; all pleasure seemed to her sacrilege toward the dead; eternal woe and tears she then thought was the just tribute she should pay to innocence so blasted and destroyed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “despond”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + pon (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: The Vale of Chamounix and Mont Blanc were Romantic pilgrimage sites; Percy Shelley wrote 'Mont Blanc' (1816).

significance: The sublime landscape mirrors Victor's mind: grand, cold and overwhelming.
discussionQuestions: How does the mountain landscape reflect Victor's feelings?
Where does setting appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the sublime power of nature?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter IX,” how does Shelley show despair and the sublime? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter IX develops the idea of despair and the sublime. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses setting in Chapter IX to complicate the reader's understanding of despair and the sublime. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter IX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of despair and the sublime responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter IX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of despair and the sublime. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: Our house was the house of mourning. My father’s health was deeply shaken by the horror of the recent events. Elizabeth was sad and desponding; she no longer took delight in her ordinary occupations; all pleasure seemed to her sacrilege toward the dead; eternal woe and tears she then thought was the just tribute she should pay to innocence so blasted and destroyed. She was no longer that happy creature, who in earlier youth wandered with me on the banks of the lake, and talked with ecstasy of our future prospects. The first of those sorrows which are sent to wean us from the earth, had visited her, and its dimming influence quenched her dearest smiles.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter IX”?

annotationFocus.label: Imagery

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How does the mountain landscape reflect Victor's feelings? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are overhangs, lulling, glaciers, perpetrate, avalanche. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “I passed the bridge of Pélissier, where the ravine, which the river forms, opened before me, and I began to ascend the mountain that overhangs it.” Webster's says: To impend or hang over. Now the word history: “overhang”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “lull”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “glacier”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The Vale of Chamounix and Mont Blanc were Romantic pilgrimage sites; Percy Shelley wrote 'Mont Blanc' (1816). Why does this chapter matter? The sublime landscape mirrors Victor's mind: grand, cold and overwhelming. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for setting.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see setting, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to despair and the sublime.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Setting, Imagery, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of setting. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Our house was the house of mourning. My father’s health was deeply shaken by the horror of the recent events. Elizabeth was sad and desponding; she no longer took delight in her ordinary occupations; all pleasure seemed to her sacrilege toward the dead; eternal woe and tears she then thought was the just tribute she should pay to innocence so blasted and destroyed. She was no longer that happy creature, who in earlier youth wandered with me on the banks of the lake, and talked with ecstasy of our future prospects. The first of those sorrows which are sent to wean us from the earth, had visited her, and its dimming influence quenched her dearest smiles.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Setting, Imagery, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter IX,” how does Shelley show despair and the sublime? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about despair and the sublime, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how setting shapes despair and the sublime. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
